learn.hook: Sociology arrived in India while the British still ruled it. Indian scholars soon asked a sharp question: can a discipline born in Europe explain a society like ours?
points: Sociology in India began under colonial rule. It was first taught at the University of Bombay from 1919; in the 1920s the universities of Calcutta and Lucknow also started teaching it.

Early Indian sociologists faced questions such as: What is colonial modernity? Is social anthropology (Western study of 'other' cultures) relevant when Indians study their own society? What role can sociology play in building a new nation?

Each founder 'Indianised' the discipline in a distinct way: Ghurye through caste and tribe, D.P. Mukerji through tradition, A.R. Desai through Marxism and the state, M.N. Srinivas through village fieldwork.
We study the founders critically, not as unquestionable authorities, so that later generations can build on and revise their work.

example.q: Why was 'social anthropology' an awkward fit for Indian scholars studying India?
steps: Western anthropology studied distant 'primitive' others.
Indian scholars were studying their own society, often their own region or community.
They had to rethink the subject's assumptions and adapt it to Indian realities.
This is part of 'Indianising' the discipline.
example.answer: Because it was built to study distant 'others', while Indians were studying their own society; they had to adapt it.

learn.reallife: The University of Mumbai's Department of Sociology, among the oldest in India, traces its roots to 1919, when sociology began to be taught at Bombay.

topics.title: The pioneers: Ananthakrishna Iyer, Sarat Chandra Roy and the administrators

learn.hook: A clerk in Cochin and a lawyer in Ranchi never planned to become famous anthropologists. Curiosity, and the people around them, changed their careers.
points: Many early Indian anthropologists entered the field almost by accident, without formal training.

L.K. Ananthakrishna Iyer (1861–1937) began as a clerk, then a school and college teacher in Cochin. He volunteered to help with an ethnographic survey of Cochin State, became a recognised scholar, and helped set up the first post-graduate anthropology department in India at the University of Calcutta.

Sarat Chandra Roy (1871–1942) was a lawyer in Ranchi who became an official interpreter in court. Wanting to understand the tribal people whose cases he handled, he studied the Oraon, Munda and Kharia, and founded the journal Man in India, the earliest journal of its kind in India.
British administrator-anthropologists, such as H.H. Risley, Edgar Thurston, J.H. Hutton and William Crooke, conducted surveys and censuses, partly to help colonial administration.
Exam skill: explain how Iyer and Roy came to practise social anthropology.

example.q: Why did Sarat Chandra Roy start studying tribal societies?
steps: He worked as a lawyer and court interpreter in Ranchi.
He had to interpret tribal customs and laws in legal cases.
To do this well, he studied tribal culture and society in depth.
His interest grew into lifelong ethnographic research.
example.answer: His court work required understanding tribal customs, which led him to systematic ethnography.

learn.reallife: Ranchi today is the capital of Jharkhand, a state formed in 2000, home to the Munda, Oraon and other communities whom Roy studied a century earlier.

topics.title: G.S. Ghurye: founder of institutional sociology

learn.hook: For 35 years one man headed India's first post-graduate sociology department and trained a whole generation of sociologists. His name: Govind Sadashiv Ghurye.
points: G.S. Ghurye (1893–1983) is regarded as the founder of institutionalised sociology in India. He headed the sociology department at Bombay University for 35 years (1924–1959).
He founded the Indian Sociological Society and its journal Sociological Bulletin.
He studied at Cambridge under W.H.R. Rivers and A.C. Haddon; his Ph.D. thesis was published as Caste and Race in India (1932).
Influences on his work: diffusionism (the idea that cultural traits spread from one culture to others), Orientalist scholarship on Hindu religion and texts, and nationalism.

example.q: Why is Ghurye called the founder of 'institutionalised' sociology, rather than the first person to study Indian society?
steps: Others (administrators, Iyer, Roy) had studied Indian society before him.
Ghurye built institutions: a long-running department, a professional society and a journal.
Institutions train students and sustain the discipline beyond one person.
So his key contribution was making sociology a lasting academic field.
example.answer: Because he built the department, society and journal that made sociology a lasting discipline in India.

learn.reallife: The Indian Sociological Society, which Ghurye founded, still holds the All India Sociological Conference, bringing together sociologists from across the country.

learn.hook: Should India's tribal communities be protected from the outside world, or brought into the national mainstream? This question split scholars in the 1930s and 40s, and still matters today.
points: Protectionist view (many British administrator-anthropologists; Verrier Elwin was its best-known voice): tribes were distinct, vulnerable communities who needed protection from exploitation by traders, moneylenders and the wider Hindu society; hence a policy of keeping them relatively separate.
Nationalist view: the British were using protection to keep tribes apart and 'divide and rule'; tribes should be integrated into the Indian mainstream and share in development.
Ghurye argued tribes were 'backward Hindus' rather than distinct cultural groups, since they had long interacted with Hindu society and were further behind in the same process of assimilation.
The debate connects to later issues: tribal movements, the creation of states such as Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh (2000), and displacement by dams, mines and industries.
Exam skill: state the arguments on both sides of the tribal debate.

example.q: Lay out both sides of the tribal debate in a table-like comparison.
steps: Protectionists: tribes are distinct; contact brings exploitation and cultural loss; protect and keep apart.
Nationalists (incl. Ghurye): separation is a colonial tactic; tribes have long interacted with Hindu society; integrate them.
Ghurye's specific claim: tribes are 'backward Hindus'.
Today: debates on autonomy, development and displacement continue.
example.answer: Protectionists favoured isolation to prevent exploitation; nationalists, including Ghurye, favoured integration, with Ghurye calling tribes 'backward Hindus'.

learn.reallife: The Fifth and Sixth Schedules of the Constitution and the Forest Rights Act, 2006 reflect ongoing efforts to balance protection of tribal rights with development.

topics.title: Risley's racial theory and Ghurye's critique

learn.hook: Colonial officials once measured noses and skulls to rank castes by 'race'. Ghurye took their own data and showed the theory did not hold for most of India.
points: H.H. Risley, a colonial administrator, argued that caste originated in race. Using anthropometry (measurement of the human body, e.g. nose width and head shape), he claimed upper castes were of Aryan origin and lower castes of non-Aryan origin.
Ghurye did not reject the data entirely but showed Risley's thesis was only partially correct.
It broadly applied only to north India ('Hindustan proper'); in other regions, the anthropometric differences between castes were small, suggesting long mixing of groups.
Ghurye also pointed out that caste-wise averages could hide wide variation within each caste.
Today, race-based explanations of caste are rejected in sociology; caste is understood as a social institution.

example.q: How did Ghurye use Risley's own type of evidence against him?
steps: Risley: body measurements show upper castes are 'Aryan', lower 'non-Aryan'.
Ghurye examined anthropometric data region by region.
Clear differences appeared broadly only in north India.
Elsewhere castes differed little, so caste could not simply be a matter of race.
example.answer: He showed that the anthropometric pattern held broadly only for north India, so race could not explain caste across India.

learn.reallife: Modern genetic studies of Indian populations also show long histories of mixing among groups, consistent with the view that caste is a social, not a racial, institution.

learn.hook: Ghurye didn't give a one-line definition of caste. He listed six features that, taken together, describe how the caste system worked.
points: 1. Segmental division: society is divided into closed, mutually exclusive segments (castes), membership fixed by birth.
2. Hierarchical division: castes are ranked from 'pure' to 'impure'. 3. Restrictions on social interaction, especially on sharing food, based on ideas of purity and pollution.
4. Differential rights and duties for different castes (in religion, dress, residence and other areas). 5. Restricted choice of occupation: occupations were hereditary.
6. Strict restrictions on marriage: caste endogamy (marrying within the caste), often with exogamy rules within it.

Glossary: anthropometry (body measurement), assimilation (absorption into a larger group), endogamy, exogamy, laissez-faire (minimal state interference in the economy), living tradition, welfare state.

(b) hereditary trade: restricted choice of occupation.
(c) food rules based on purity: restriction on social interaction.

topics.title: D.P. Mukerji on change: shruti, smriti and anubhava

learn.hook: Kabir never wrote a scripture, yet his couplets changed how millions thought about caste and god. D.P. Mukerji would call that the power of anubhava, experience.
points: Mukerji argued that change in India comes through group and caste experience rather than class conflict, because class consciousness was weak and caste and group identities were strong.
Indian tradition recognises three principles: shruti (what is heard, revealed scripture), smriti (what is remembered, texts and codes based on tradition) and anubhava (personal experience).
Of these, anubhava is the revolutionary principle: experience can challenge established ideas.
In practice, it is the generalised anubhava, the collective experience of groups, that drives change; e.g. the Bhakti saints and Sufi saints whose experiences challenged orthodoxy and hierarchy.
Activity skill: trace changes in games, festivals or dress across generations in your family to see how traditions adapt.

(c) personal experience: anubhava, the revolutionary principle.

topics.title: A.R. Desai and the welfare state

learn.hook: Many governments call themselves welfare states. A.R. Desai, a Marxist sociologist, set out tests to check whether they really were.
points: A.R. Desai (1915–1994) was a Marxist sociologist, known for his book Social Background of Indian Nationalism (1948), which analysed Indian nationalism using Marxist ideas.

He described the welfare state as having three features: (1) a positive state that actively uses its powers to implement social policies (not laissez-faire); (2) a democratic state, with democracy considered essential; (3) a mixed economy, where private and public enterprises co-exist.

Desai's tests of a welfare state: freedom from poverty, social discrimination and insecurity for all citizens; removal of inequalities of income through redistribution; transforming the economy so that community needs come before profit; stable development free from economic booms and busts; and employment for all.

example.q: Apply two of Desai's tests to a country that has free schools but high unemployment and growing income inequality.
steps: Test: employment for all. High unemployment: fails.
Test: reducing income inequality. Growing inequality: fails.
Free schools help reduce insecurity, but overall the state falls short.
example.answer: It fails at least two of Desai's tests (employment for all, reducing income inequality).

learn.reallife: India's directive principles, schemes like the Public Distribution System and MGNREGA, and public sector undertakings are often discussed as welfare-state features against Desai's tests.

learn.hook: After applying his tests to Britain, the USA and other advanced countries, Desai reached a bold verdict: the welfare state is largely a myth.
points: Desai found that even advanced capitalist countries such as Britain and the USA failed many of his tests: poverty, inequality and unemployment persisted, and economic booms and busts continued.
He concluded that the welfare state is largely a myth: it does not deliver on its promises under capitalism.
He also criticised communist states, which in his view did not adequately protect democracy and freedoms, even if they provided some economic security.
Activity skill: list state services in your area (schools, hospitals, rations, transport) and ask how different classes use and view them.
Exam skill: explain the welfare state and Desai's criticism of it.

example.q: A rich family uses private hospitals; a poor family depends on a government hospital with long queues. What would Desai's approach highlight?
steps: Different classes relate differently to state services.
If public services are weak, the poor gain little security.
Unequal access suggests the state is not removing class inequality.
This supports Desai's view that the welfare state falls short.
example.answer: It would highlight class differences in access, supporting Desai's critique that welfare promises are not fully met.

learn.reallife: Comparing how a family uses Ayushman Bharat cards, ration shops and government schools with how another uses private alternatives is a ready-made Desai-style class analysis.

learn.hook: In 1970, a fire destroyed M.N. Srinivas's field notes on the village of Rampura. He rewrote the village from memory, and The Remembered Village became a classic.
points: M.N. Srinivas (1916–1999) studied under Ghurye at Bombay and then at Oxford under A.R. Radcliffe-Brown and E.E. Evans-Pritchard.

He built major institutions: the sociology department at M.S. University of Baroda, the Department of Sociology at the Delhi School of Economics, and the Institute for Social and Economic Change in Bangalore.
Village studies were a central field of Indian sociology in the 1950s and 1960s, with scholars such as Srinivas (Rampura, Mysore), S.C. Dube and D.N. Majumdar.
Concepts linked to Srinivas include the dominant caste and Sanskritisation (a lower caste adopting the customs and practices of higher castes to raise its status).
Village studies showed the value of ethnographic fieldwork and documented rapid change in rural India as a new nation developed.

example.q: Why were village studies so important for Indian sociology in the 1950s and 60s?
steps: Most Indians lived in villages, so villages were central to understanding India.
Fieldwork gave first-hand evidence instead of colonial stereotypes.
They recorded how land reform, development and democracy were changing rural life.
They trained a generation in ethnographic methods.
example.answer: They used fieldwork to give first-hand evidence about rural India and documented change in a new nation.

learn.reallife: About two-thirds of Indians still lived in rural areas in the 2011 Census, so village-level research remains essential for understanding India.

topics.title: The village debate: Srinivas versus Dumont

learn.hook: Is the Indian village a real community, or just a place where different castes happen to live? Two great scholars, M.N. Srinivas and Louis Dumont, disagreed sharply.
points: Louis Dumont, a French social anthropologist, argued that the village was merely a collection of people living in one place; caste was the real social unit and institution.
Srinivas argued that the village was a real and relevant social unit, with its own unity and identity.
Srinivas also showed that the village had changed historically and was never the unchanging, self-sufficient 'little republic' described by some British administrators.
Village studies thus corrected colonial stereotypes and showed rural India as dynamic.
Clues that a place is a village: most people work in agriculture, the population is small and less dense, and relations are face-to-face.
Activity skills: identify the clues that tell you a place is a village; discuss whether urban Indians still care about villages.

example.q: A villager says, 'I am a Brahmin, but first I am from Rampura.' Whose view does this support?
steps: Dumont: caste is the real unit, village is a mere collection.
Srinivas: the village is a real unit with its own identity.
The villager identifies strongly with the village.
This supports Srinivas's view.
example.answer: It supports Srinivas: the village is a meaningful unit of identity.

learn.reallife: Many city dwellers still return to their native villages for festivals, weddings and elections, a living link that keeps the 'village versus city' debate alive.
